title: Given a set of positive numbers, determine if there is a subset whose sum equals a given target S. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack boolean DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Subset Sum (Decide if a Subset Reaches an Exact Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. We ask whether any subset of the numbers adds up to an exact target S. A boolean dynamic programming array marks which sums are reachable, filled by considering each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of individual transaction amounts and wants to know whether some combination of them exactly matches a disputed figure. Subset Sum checks, without trying every combination by brute force, whether any subset reaches that exact amount.
s1_definition.oneliner: A boolean array over target sums, filled once per number, answers can-we-hit-exactly-S.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. We ask whether any subset of the numbers adds up to an exact target S. A boolean dynamic programming array marks which sums are reachable, filled by considering each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a list of individual transaction amounts and wants to know whether some combination of them exactly matches a disputed figure. Subset Sum checks, without trying every combination by brute force, whether any subset reaches that exact amount.

**One line to remember:** A boolean array over target sums, filled once per number, answers can-we-hit-exactly-S.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a boolean array `dp[t]` where `t` ranges from zero to the target S, and `dp[t]` is true when some subset sums to `t`. The base case is `dp[0] = true` because choosing nothing sums to zero.

For each number we sweep `t` from S down to the number and set `dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num]`. If `t` was already reachable we keep it, otherwise it becomes reachable when `t - num` was reachable, meaning we add the current number to an existing subset. A concrete update is `for (int t = S; t >= num; t--) dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num];`. The final answer is `dp[S]`.

Senior nuance: the high-to-low sweep is what makes this 0/1 rather than unbounded, because it prevents a single number from being added to itself within the same pass. We can stop early once `dp[S]` is true, and if the target exceeds the total of all numbers we can answer false without any DP.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India investigates a disputed statement where a customer claims a specific total was charged, and the fraud team needs to know whether some subset of the actual individual charges adds up exactly to the disputed figure. Trying every combination explicitly would be far too slow for a long charge list. This is exactly how Subset Sum works: it decides exact reachability with a boolean DP.

The code defines a `DisputeCheckService` exposing `hasSubsetSum(charges, target)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` runs it over a charge list and a disputed target and logs whether the target is reachable.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four charges 120, 75, 200, 45 with a disputed target of 165.

Step 1 — We build a boolean array of length 166, all false except dp[0] which is true. Only the sum zero is reachable at the start.

Step 2 — Process 120. Sweeping 165 down to 120, dp[120] becomes true from dp[0]. Reachable sums are zero and 120.

Step 3 — Process 75. dp[195] is out of range; within range dp[120 plus 75 equals 195] is skipped, but dp[75] becomes true from dp[0]. Reachable sums are zero, 75, 120.

Step 4 — Process 200. Two hundred exceeds the target range, so the inner loop does nothing because the loop condition t at least 200 never holds within a target of 165. Reachable sums are unchanged.

Step 5 — Process 45. dp[165] becomes true from dp[120], because 120 plus 45 equals 165. We stop early. The disputed figure is exactly reachable as 120 plus 45, shown below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:59:40 PM com.bank.dispute.service.DisputeCheckService hasSubsetSum
INFO: Exact subset for target 165 = true
Oct 27, 2026 8:59:40 PM com.bank.dispute.DisputeCheckApplication main
INFO: Can charges sum exactly to Rs.165? true
```

```
    │ process 120: reachable {0,120}

    │ process 45 : dp[165] via dp[120] ← early exit

  dp[165] = true  (subset 120+45 = 165)
  Output: reachable = true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. The question is simply whether any subset of the given numbers adds up to an exact target, and I answer it with a boolean dynamic programming array where each slot records whether that sum is reachable. I seed the array with the sum zero reachable through the empty subset, then for every number I mark new sums reachable by extending sums that were already reachable with that number added.

The correctness hinge is the sweep direction. I iterate the target from high down to the current number so that, within a single number's pass, I never add that number to a sum it just created, which is what keeps each number usable at most once. This is the identical device that distinguishes 0/1 Knapsack from the unbounded variant. I also exit as soon as the target becomes reachable and I can reject instantly if the target exceeds the total of all numbers.

At the National Bank of India I used this in dispute reconciliation, where a customer claimed a specific total was charged and the fraud team needed to know whether some subset of the real individual charges summed exactly to that disputed figure. I ran the boolean subset-sum DP over the charge list toward the disputed target. Explaining that the answer is reachability rather than value, that the high-to-low sweep enforces using each charge once, and that the cost is N times the target is what shows an interviewer I understand the 0/1 Knapsack feasibility pattern.
